title: Camera Fundamentals: Resolution, Framerate & the Exposure Triangle
html:
Resolution: capture big, deliver smart

Resolution is the pixel count of each frame. The common drone ladder is 1080p (1920x1080), 2.7K (2720x1530), 4K (3840x2160), and on higher-end birds 5.1K/6K. More pixels buys you two real things: delivery sharpness for 4K screens, and reframing headroom — shoot 4K, deliver 1080p, and you can punch in or stabilize a crop without softening the image. The cost is file size, heat, and storage. A practical rule: shoot 4K as your default; only drop to 2.7K/1080p when you specifically need a higher framerate the sensor can't sustain at 4K.

Framerate and the feel of motion

Framerate (fps) is how many frames are recorded per second. It controls motion feel, not slowness by itself.

  • 24 fps (23.976) — the cinematic standard. Slight motion blur, filmic cadence.
  • 25 fps — PAL regions; broadcast deliverable in Europe.
  • 30 fps (29.97) — clean, slightly more 'video' look; common for online content.
  • 60 fps — captured to be slowed to 40% in a 24p timeline for smooth slow-motion, or played at 60p for hyper-real motion.
  • 120 fps — dramatic 5x slow motion at 24p; needs a lot of light.

The key concept: capture framerate and timeline framerate are separate. To get slow motion, shoot at a high framerate (e.g. 60fps) and interpret/conform it onto a 24fps timeline. 60 into 24 = 40% speed; 120 into 24 = 20% speed.

The exposure triangle on a drone

Three controls set brightness, but on most camera drones one is fixed:

ControlRange on dronesTrade-off
ApertureOften FIXED (e.g. f/2.8), or f/2.8-f/11 on Mavic 3 / Air 3 styleIf fixed, you cannot use it to dim light — use ND filters
ISO100 base, up to 6400+Higher ISO = more noise/grain; keep near base
Shutter1/8000 to several secondsControls motion blur — locked by the 180° rule for video

Because shutter is locked for cinematic motion (next lesson) and aperture is often fixed, your only clean brightness lever in bright daylight becomes the ND filter — that's why pros carry a filter set. Keep ISO at base 100 whenever light allows; only raise it in low light, accepting noise.

Insight.
Think of exposure in this order for video: lock framerate, set shutter via the 180° rule, set ISO to 100, then add ND filters until the image is correctly exposed. Aperture comes in only if your drone has a variable iris.

Bit depth, codec and color

Beyond resolution, two numbers decide grading flexibility. Bit depth (8-bit vs 10-bit) sets how many tones per channel: 8-bit = 16.7M colors and bands easily in skies; 10-bit = ~1.07B colors and grades cleanly. Codec/bitrate (H.264 vs H.265, e.g. 100Mbps vs 150Mbps) sets compression quality. For any serious grade, choose 10-bit H.265 at the highest bitrate your card sustains (use a V30/U3 card or better).

Flight safety.
Changing camera settings mid-air pulls your eyes off the aircraft. Set resolution/framerate on the ground, hover in a stable position to tweak exposure, and keep a visual observer if you're heads-down in the app.
▸Hands-On

Feel how framerate changes motion.

  1. Capture or find three clips of the same moving subject at 24, 30, and 60 fps.
  2. Drop all three onto a 24fps timeline; conform the 60fps one to 40% speed.
  3. Write one sentence each: how the 24fps feels cinematic, how 30fps feels, and how the slowed 60fps reads for slow motion.
  4. Note which you'd pick for a moody reveal vs a sports flyby and why.

title: Shutter Speed, ND Filters & the 180° Rule
html:
Why motion blur matters

Each video frame is a short exposure. If the shutter is very fast (e.g. 1/2000s), every frame is a crisp frozen snapshot and motion looks stuttery and 'gamey' — this is the classic mistake that screams amateur drone footage. If the shutter is slower, each frame contains a little smear of movement, and when 24 of those play per second your eye reads it as smooth, natural motion. The goal is the right amount of blur.

The 180° shutter rule

The film-world standard is the 180-degree shutter, which produces a shutter speed of 1 / (2 x framerate). Cameras don't show degrees, they show a fraction, so memorize the math:

Framerate2 x fpsTarget shutter (nearest setting)
24 fps481/50s
25 fps501/50s
30 fps601/60s
60 fps1201/120s (or 1/125)
120 fps2401/240s (or 1/250)

Cameras rarely have exactly 1/48, so use the nearest available step (1/50). Going one stop faster (a '90-degree' look, e.g. 1/100 at 24fps) is a deliberate choice for crunchy action shots; just know you're breaking the rule on purpose.

The bright-daylight problem

Here's the conflict: at 24fps you must hold shutter at ~1/50s. But 1/50s at ISO 100 on a sunny day is wildly overexposed — the image blows out to white. You can't speed up the shutter (that breaks the 180° rule), you can't lower ISO below 100, and aperture is often fixed. The solution is to put sunglasses on the lens: a neutral density (ND) filter.

Choosing ND strength

ND filters are rated by how many stops of light they cut. Each stop halves the light. Naming varies — ND4/ND8/ND16/ND32/ND64 (the number = light reduction factor) where ND4 = 2 stops, ND8 = 3, ND16 = 4, ND32 = 5, ND64 = 6.

ConditionTypical NDStops
Overcast / heavy cloudsND42
Hazy sun, golden hourND83
Bright partly cloudyND164
Full bright sunND325
Intense sun on snow/water/sandND646

Workflow in the air: lock framerate and the matching shutter, set ISO 100, then screw on the ND that brings the exposure meter to 0 (no blinkies/clipping on highlights). If still overexposed, go darker (higher ND); if dim, go lighter. Many kits sell as ND8/16/32/64 packs precisely because that span covers most daylight.

Insight.
Adjustable/variable ND filters exist but can introduce an 'X' cross-pattern at extreme settings and color cast. For critical work, fixed-strength NDs are more reliable; carry the set and swap on the ground.
Prop safety.
Many drone NDs clip over the gimbal. Always confirm the filter is fully seated before takeoff — a filter shed in flight can hit the props or jam the gimbal. Power off and verify the gimbal moves freely after fitting.
▸Hands-On

Calculate shutter and pick ND for three scenarios.

  1. Scenario A: 24fps, full bright sun. Target shutter? Likely ND?
  2. Scenario B: 60fps, golden hour. Target shutter? Likely ND?
  3. Scenario C: 30fps, overcast. Target shutter? Likely ND?
  4. Write the 180° math you used for each, then the ND you'd mount first and how you'd adjust if highlights still clip.

title: Flat & Log Color Profiles and Why They Matter
html:
What a color profile actually does

A color profile is the curve the camera applies when it converts the sensor's raw light readings into a recorded file. A standard profile (often called Normal, Vivid, or just the default) bakes in contrast, saturation, and a pleasing 'look' so the footage looks good straight out of the drone. A flat or Log profile does the opposite: it deliberately records a low-contrast, desaturated, washed-out image to preserve dynamic range — the detail in both shadows and highlights — so you can shape the look later in grading.

Flat vs Log vs standard

ProfileOut-of-camera lookDynamic rangeBest for
Standard / NormalContrasty, saturated, readyLimitedQuick delivery, social, no grading time
Flat (e.g. D-Cinelike)Low contrast, mild desatModerateLight grading, 8-bit footage
Log (e.g. D-Log, D-Log M, HLG)Very washed out, greyMaximumSerious grading, 10-bit, matching cameras

On DJI drones you'll see names like D-Cinelike (a flat-ish profile) and D-Log / D-Log M (true Log). HLG (Hybrid Log Gamma) is a hybrid that looks decent un-graded on HDR displays.

Why grey footage is good

A sensor captures more dynamic range than a standard profile can store. Log redistributes that range so highlights (bright clouds) don't clip to pure white and shadows (tree lines) don't crush to pure black. The footage looks ugly and milky on the monitor — that's expected. In post you apply contrast and color and recover detail that a standard profile would have thrown away. This is how you keep a bright sky AND a properly lit foreground in the same shot.

The catch: bit depth and noise

Log needs room to be stretched back out. On 8-bit footage, aggressive Log grading exposes banding (visible steps in skies) because there simply aren't enough tonal values. 10-bit Log grades cleanly. This is the single most important pairing: if your drone only shoots 8-bit, a flat profile like D-Cinelike is often the smarter choice than full D-Log. If you have 10-bit, D-Log unlocks the most flexibility. Log also amplifies shadow noise, so you must expose Log a touch brighter (ETTR — expose to the right) and protect the shadows.

Insight.
Rule of thumb: shoot Log/flat when you (a) have time to grade, (b) shoot 10-bit, and (c) face high-contrast scenes or need to match another camera. Shoot standard when you need footage usable immediately with no post.

LUTs: the translator

Because Log looks wrong, manufacturers provide a LUT (Look-Up Table) — a conversion file that maps Log back to a normal Rec.709 look. A 'conversion LUT' (e.g. DJI's D-Log to Rec.709) is your neutral starting point in the edit; a 'creative LUT' adds a stylized look on top. Apply the conversion LUT first, then grade.

Field check.
Log monitoring is deceptive — the washed-out preview makes it hard to judge exposure by eye. Use the histogram or zebras, not the picture, and never adjust framing so much that you fly unsafely while squinting at a grey screen.
▸Hands-On

Decide when each profile wins.

  1. Find or shoot the same high-contrast scene in a standard profile and a Log/flat profile.
  2. Apply the conversion LUT to the Log clip and compare recovered sky/shadow detail vs the standard clip.
  3. Write two scenarios: one where standard is the better capture choice, one where Log is — and tie each to bit depth and grading time.

title: The Gimbal: Mechanical Stabilization vs FPV Smoothing
html:
Two completely different ways to get smooth footage

Camera drones (DJI Mavic/Air) and FPV drones (cinewhoops, freestyle quads) both produce buttery footage, but through opposite philosophies. Understanding the difference tells you which tool to grab for a given shot.

Mechanical gimbals: isolate the camera

A camera drone carries the lens on a 3-axis mechanical gimbal — three brushless motors that actively counter-rotate on the pitch, roll, and yaw axes. An IMU senses the drone's every twitch and the motors instantly move the camera the opposite amount, physically holding the lens steady in space while the airframe jitters around it. The result is a locked-off, tripod-smooth horizon no matter what the wind does. You control framing by tilting the gimbal (pitch) independently of where the drone flies.

  • Pitch — tilt up/down, your main framing control (e.g. -90° straight down for top-down).
  • Roll — keeps the horizon level automatically.
  • Yaw — assists with smooth pans; coordinated with the drone's own rotation.

Mechanical gimbals give a detached, floating, observational feel. The camera glides; the world is presented calmly. This is the look of real estate, landscape, and most commercial aerial work.

FPV: no gimbal, fix it differently

An FPV cinewhoop usually has the camera hard-mounted (or on a single soft mount/TPU damping) — there is no motorized gimbal isolating it. So how is FPV footage smooth? Three layers:

  1. Pilot skill — smooth stick inputs and acro flying that the camera follows directly. The camera is the aircraft's attitude.
  2. Soft mounting — TPU/foam dampers absorb high-frequency motor vibration ('jello').
  3. Electronic stabilization in post — Gyroflow or DJI/GoPro embedded gyro data warps each frame to cancel rotation, using recorded gyroscope logs. This removes jitter while keeping the dynamic motion.

The FPV look is immersive, kinetic, connected — the camera dives, banks, and rolls because the whole aircraft does. It feels like a bird, not a tripod.

AspectMechanical gimbal droneFPV cinewhoop
StabilizationActive motors isolate cameraPilot + soft mount + post (Gyroflow)
HorizonAlways level automaticallyBanks/rolls with the aircraft
Motion feelFloating, detached, calmImmersive, fast, connected
Tight spacesLimited, cautiousExcellent — fly-throughs, dives
Latency/controlPosition-based, forgivingDirect, demands skill
Insight.
A useful mental model: a gimbal drone shows you a place from outside; an FPV drone takes you through it. Many edits intercut both — a calm gimbal establisher then an FPV fly-through for energy.
Gimbal care.
Always remove the gimbal clamp before powering on, and never force the gimbal by hand while it's powered — you can strip a motor or corrupt calibration. If footage shows a tilted horizon on a gimbal drone, recalibrate the gimbal and IMU on a level surface before blaming the camera.
▸Hands-On

Compare the two looks directly.

  1. Find one gimbal-drone clip and one FPV cinewhoop clip of similar environments.
  2. Note how the horizon behaves in each, and whether the camera tilts with banking.
  3. Write 3 sentences contrasting the motion feel and name one shot each is better at.

title: Core Shot Types: Orbit, Reveal, Fly-Through, Dolly, Top-Down & Parallax
html:
The staple six

Almost every aerial edit is built from a small vocabulary of repeatable moves. Master these six and you can cover any location. Stick references assume Mode 2 (left stick = throttle/yaw, right stick = pitch/roll).

1. Orbit (POI / circle)

The drone circles a subject while the camera stays pointed at it. Creates rotation and reveals all sides — great for hero objects, towers, people. Sticks: gentle constant roll (right stick left/right) to arc sideways + opposite yaw (left stick) to keep the nose/camera on the subject. Most camera drones automate this as 'Point of Interest' mode — set radius, speed, and altitude. Manual orbits look more organic but take practice to keep the radius constant.

2. Reveal

Hide the subject behind a foreground object (ridge, tree, building) then move to expose it. Tilt reveal: camera pitched down at terrain, then ascend while tilting up to reveal a distant vista. Pull-back reveal: start tight on subject, fly backward and up so the surroundings 'grow' around it. Sticks: combine slow backward pitch (right stick down) with throttle up (left stick up) and a gentle gimbal tilt.

3. Fly-through

Pass through a gap — a doorway, arch, tree line, under a bridge. The signature FPV/cinewhoop shot; risky on big camera drones. Sticks: steady forward pitch, precise altitude and lateral trim. Scout the gap, check for prop clearance, and never fly through anything you haven't confirmed is clear of wires.

4. Dolly

A straight, smooth translation — forward, backward, or sideways (a 'truck') — like a camera on rails. The most cinematic establisher. Sticks: single-axis input only; resist mixing channels. Forward dolly = constant gentle forward pitch at fixed altitude. Sideways dolly past a subject creates strong parallax.

5. Top-down (bird's eye)

Gimbal pitched to -90°, looking straight down. Turns the world into graphic, abstract patterns — roads, fields, coastlines, crowds. Variants: static hover, slow descent ('God's eye drop'), or a slow rotating top-down (yaw spin) for a hypnotic spiral. Sticks: set gimbal to -90, then translate slowly or add slow yaw.

6. Parallax

Not a path so much as an effect: fly laterally past a foreground object while a background sits far behind. The near object slides quickly, the far one barely moves, creating powerful 3D depth. Achieved with a sideways dolly or an orbit with a strong foreground element. The closer the foreground, the stronger the parallax.

ShotPrimary inputFeels like
OrbitRoll + counter-yawShowcase / rotation
RevealPitch + throttle + tiltSurprise / scale
Fly-throughForward pitch, preciseImmersion
DollySingle-axis translateCinematic glide
Top-downGimbal -90 + slow moveAbstract / map
ParallaxLateral pass w/ foregroundDepth / 3D
Insight.
Slower is almost always more cinematic. Fly at 30-50% of the speed that feels right in the moment, and start recording 3 seconds before the move and stop 3 seconds after — you need handles for editing.
Fly-through safety.
Fly-throughs and low reveals are where crashes happen. Always do a slow dry-run pass first, watch for thin wires (often invisible on screen), keep a spotter, and never thread a gap you couldn't safely walk through.
▸Hands-On

Storyboard the six shots for one location.

  1. Pick a real or imagined location (park, building, coastline).
  2. For each of the six shots, sketch the drone path (top-view arrow) and the camera framing.
  3. Note the stick movement and gimbal angle for each.
  4. Order them into a 30-second sequence: which opens, which is the climax.

title: Planning a Shoot & Storyboarding
html:
The shoot is won before you fly

Great aerial work is 80% planning. Showing up and 'seeing what happens' wastes battery, light, and often your one legal window. A professional plan covers four pillars: location, light, shots, and safety/airspace.

1. Scout the location

Use satellite maps and apps before you arrive. Identify the best subject angles, obstacles (towers, wires, trees), launch/recovery spots, and where the sun will be. Tools: Google Earth for 3D terrain, an app like PhotoPills or Sun Surveyor to see exactly where the sun rises/sets and how shadows fall at your shoot time. Visit in person if possible — wires and 'no drone' signage rarely show on satellite.

2. Time the light

The two best windows are the golden hour (the ~hour after sunrise and before sunset — warm, low, long shadows, soft) and the blue hour (the ~20-30 min before sunrise/after sunset — cool, even, city lights glow). Midday sun is flat and harsh; avoid it for hero shots. Build your shot list around the light: shoot east-facing subjects at sunrise, west-facing at sunset. Arrive 30+ minutes early to set up, calibrate, and do a test flight before the light peaks.

3. Build a shot list and storyboard

Translate the story into specific named shots (from the previous lesson). For each line specify: shot type, subject, altitude, gimbal angle, move direction, and duration. Sketch the path. A simple shot list might read:

shotlist.txt
# SHOT TYPE SUBJECT ALT GIMBAL MOVE DUR 01 Dolly fwd coast road 40m -15 forward 12s 02 Reveal lighthouse 20-80m -30/0 ascend+tilt 15s 03 Orbit lighthouse 50m -20 CW 360 30s 04 Top-down tide pools 60m -90 slow truck 10s 05 Parallax rock+sea 25m -10 lateral L 12s # golden hour starts 19:42, sunset 20:31 -- shoot 01-03 first

4. Safety and airspace check

Before any flight, confirm you are legal and safe for this exact place and day. This is not optional.

  • Airspace: check controlled airspace and request authorization if needed. In the US use the FAA B4UFLY app or a LAANC provider (Aloft, Avision) for instant authorization near airports. Verify TFRs (temporary flight restrictions).
  • Registration & rules: ensure your drone is registered and you fly within current rules (altitude limit, line of sight, no flying over people/moving vehicles unless authorized, Remote ID compliance).
  • Weather: check wind (gusts especially), precipitation, temperature (cold kills LiPo performance), and KP index for GPS. Use UAV Forecast or similar.
  • Site: note people, wildlife, private property, and emergency landing zones.
Verify current rules.
Drone regulations change frequently and vary by country and locality. Always confirm the latest FAA (or your national authority) and local rules, registration, Remote ID, and any site-specific permits before flying. This lesson is general guidance, not legal advice.
Insight.
Always plan a backup: a second location or a 'plan B for clouds/wind', plus spare batteries (golden hour is short — carry at least 3 charged packs) and ND filters for the expected light.
Pre-flight.
Run a checklist every time: props secure, battery seated and charged, gimbal clamp off, IMU/compass calibrated if location changed, home point set, RTH altitude above obstacles, SD card present and formatted.
▸Hands-On

Produce a complete shoot plan for a real location.

  1. Pick a real, legal-to-fly location near you and scout it on satellite + sun app.
  2. Write a shot list of 5+ named shots with altitude, gimbal, move, duration.
  3. Record golden-hour times and which shots you'll shoot first for the light.
  4. Do an airspace check (B4UFLY/LAANC), note weather/wind, and write a backup plan and battery count.

title: Drone Photography: HDR, Panoramas & Art vs Mapping
html:
Stills are a different discipline

Aerial photography rewards patience over motion. You hover, you compose carefully, and you capture more data than one frame can hold — then blend in post. Two techniques do the heavy lifting: HDR bracketing and panorama stitching.

Shoot RAW

For any serious photo, set the camera to RAW (DNG) not JPEG. RAW keeps the full sensor data so you can recover blown skies and crushed shadows in Lightroom/Camera Raw. JPEG bakes in choices and discards latitude. Use the lowest ISO (100), a single AF lock, and the histogram to avoid clipping.

HDR via exposure bracketing

A bright sky and a dark foreground exceed the sensor's dynamic range in one shot. Bracketing takes several frames at different exposures — for example 3 or 5 shots at -2, -1, 0, +1, +2 EV (AEB mode) — which you later merge so the dark frame keeps highlight detail and the bright frame keeps shadow detail. The result is a single image with detail everywhere.

  • Enable AEB (Auto Exposure Bracketing): 3 or 5 frames.
  • Keep the drone perfectly still — hover in low wind so frames align. Movement causes ghosting.
  • Merge in Lightroom (Photo > Photo Merge > HDR) or similar; it outputs a 32-bit DNG you then tone-map gently. Avoid the over-cooked 'HDR halo' look.

Panoramas

A panorama stitches many overlapping frames into one ultra-wide, high-resolution image. Drones automate the capture and sometimes the stitch:

Pano typeWhat it capturesUse
Wide / horizontalRow of frames left-to-rightLandscapes, coastlines
VerticalTop-to-bottom columnTall subjects, foreground-to-sky
180° / SphereGrid covering the whole viewImmersive, 'tiny planet' edits
  • Aim for ~30% overlap between frames so the stitcher has matching features.
  • Lock exposure (manual mode) across all frames — auto-exposure causes visible seams.
  • Shoot the in-app pano (auto), or capture RAW frames manually and stitch in Lightroom/PTGui/Photoshop Photomerge for maximum quality.
  • Keep the drone position fixed; only the gimbal/yaw rotates between frames.

Art vs mapping — two opposite goals

People confuse aerial photography with drone mapping; they share hardware but nothing else.

Artistic photographyMapping / survey
GoalA beautiful imageAccurate measurable data
CompositionSubjective, light/angle drivenIrrelevant — uniform coverage
CaptureFew hero frames, golden hourAutomated grid, nadir (-90°), even light
Overlap~30% for panos70-80% front/side for photogrammetry
OutputPrint / social imageOrthomosaic, 3D model, point cloud, DEM
SoftwareLightroom, PhotoshopDroneDeploy, Pix4D, WebODM

Mapping flies a programmed lawnmower pattern at fixed altitude, straight down, with heavy overlap and consistent flat lighting (midday is fine — you don't want shadows). Photogrammetry software then reconstructs geometry. Art is the opposite: dramatic low light, careful angles, few frames.

Insight.
For panoramas, shoot at base ISO and lock white balance too — a drifting WB tints frames differently and the seams glow. For HDR, 3 brackets at +/-2 EV usually beats 5 unless contrast is extreme.
Hover safety.
HDR and panos mean long hovers, often heads-down stitching shots. Watch battery (these eat time), keep clear of obstacles since you're stationary, and abort if wind picks up — drift ruins the merge and risks the aircraft.
▸Hands-On

Capture and merge an HDR set and a panorama.

  1. Set RAW, ISO 100, manual exposure. Shoot a 3- or 5-frame AEB bracket of a high-contrast scene.
  2. Shoot a horizontal panorama with ~30% overlap, locking exposure and WB.
  3. Merge the HDR in Lightroom and stitch the pano (in-app or Photomerge).
  4. Note the settings used and one fix for any ghosting or seam you saw.

title: Editing Workflow, Color Grading & Exporting
html:
A repeatable post workflow

A clean pipeline matters more than any single trick. The standard order is: ingest > organize > assemble > grade > finish > export. Editors like DaVinci Resolve (free, industry color tool), Premiere Pro, or Final Cut all follow this.

  1. Ingest & back up: copy SD card to a working drive AND a backup before touching anything. Never edit off the card.
  2. Organize: import, set the project framerate to match your footage (e.g. 24fps), label clips, and pick selects (the good takes).
  3. Assemble: cut the sequence to the music/story first, in flat/Log, focusing on pacing and order before color.
  4. Grade: after the edit is locked, do color.

Color grading Log/flat footage

Grading has two stages: correction (make it accurate/neutral) then grade (make it stylish). In Resolve this lives in the Color page using nodes; in Premiere it's Lumetri layers. A clean node tree:

node tree (Resolve)
Node 1 Conversion LUT D-Log -> Rec.709 (un-flatten) Node 2 Balance white balance + exposure to neutral Node 3 Contrast lift/gamma/gain, set black & white point Node 4 Saturation pull back over-saturated greens/blues Node 5 Creative teal-orange / warm look, creative LUT Node 6 Secondary qualify sky, boost it selectively # judge on scopes, not just your eyes

Key tools: use the waveform scope to set blacks near 0 and whites near 100 IRE without clipping; the parade (RGB) scope to remove color casts (align the three channels in the shadows for neutral). Don't grade by eye alone — monitors lie.

Common grading moves

  • Apply the manufacturer conversion LUT first so you're grading a normal image, not grey Log.
  • Fix white balance before contrast.
  • Add contrast gently — Log footage needs it, but watch for crushed shadows.
  • Slight teal in shadows + warmth in highlights is the popular cinematic 'orange-teal' look; use sparingly.
  • Match exposure across clips of the same scene so cuts don't flash.

Exporting for delivery

Export settings must match where the video will live.

DeliveryCodecResolution / fpsBitrate
YouTube / webH.264/H.2653840x2160 @ 24/30~40-50 Mbps (4K)
Instagram/socialH.2641080x1080 / 1080x1920~15-25 Mbps
Master / archiveProRes 422 HQSource res & fpsVery high (intra)

Keep the timeline framerate through to export (don't change 24 to 30). Export a high-quality master in ProRes for archive, then derive compressed versions for each platform from that master.

Insight.
Render a short test of your most graded clip and watch it on the actual target device (phone, TV) before exporting the whole project — banding and saturation often look different there. 10-bit timelines grade with far less banding than 8-bit.
▸Hands-On

Grade one Log/flat clip and export it.

  1. Import a flat/Log clip into Resolve (or your editor) onto a matching-fps timeline.
  2. Build the node/layer chain: conversion LUT, balance, contrast, saturation, creative look.
  3. Check the waveform and parade scopes; fix any clipping or color cast.
  4. Export at a specified target (e.g. 4K H.265 @ 24fps, 45 Mbps) and write down each node/layer step you used.

title: Matching Aerial to Ground Footage in a Sequence
html:
The seam you don't want the viewer to notice

A polished film intercuts aerial and ground shots so they feel like one camera in one world. When the cut jumps in color temperature, exposure, or rhythm, the audience subconsciously notices and the spell breaks. Matching happens on two axes: color and pacing.

Why aerial and ground footage differ

They're shot on different sensors with different profiles. A DJI drone in D-Log and a mirrorless camera or phone in its own Log/standard profile will have different color science, contrast, white balance, and noise. Aerial footage often has more haze and a cooler, hazier sky; ground footage is closer and richer. Your job in post is to reconcile them to a shared look.

Color matching workflow

  1. Neutralize both first. Apply each camera's conversion LUT (or correct each manually) so both clips are normal Rec.709 — not stylized. You can't match two stylized looks reliably.
  2. Pick a hero clip. Choose one clip whose look you like (often the ground shot of your subject) as the reference everyone matches to.
  3. Match on scopes. Put both clips side by side. Use the parade scope to align black points, white points, and the balance of R/G/B in shadows and highlights. Resolve's 'Shot Match' can do a first pass; refine by hand.
  4. Match white balance and skin/key tones. Drag the aerial's temperature/tint to match the ground clip's. If people are in frame, match skin tones above all.
  5. Apply the creative grade last, to the whole timeline (an adjustment/timeline-level node), so the same look sits on both — this glues them together.
match checklist
1. both clips conversion-LUT'd to Rec.709 2. black point aligned on parade (both ~0) 3. white point aligned (both <100, no clip) 4. WB matched -- compare a known neutral / sky 5. creative look on a TIMELINE node over both result: cut should be invisible color-wise

Pacing and motion matching

Color isn't enough — the movement must flow too.

  • Match motion direction: if the aerial pushes left-to-right, cut to a ground shot that continues that direction, or deliberately contrasts it.
  • Match speed/energy: a slow floating aerial cuts awkwardly into a frantic handheld ground shot. Either slow the ground clip or pick a calmer take. Conform framerates so slow-mo intent is consistent.
  • Cut on the beat: if scored, place aerial-to-ground cuts on musical hits so the rhythm carries the transition.
  • Use motivated cuts: a top-down aerial of a road can cut to a ground shot of a car on that road — the audience follows the logic.
  • Match grain/sharpness: aerial 4K can look cleaner than a noisy ground clip; add a touch of grain or soften slightly so textures match.
Insight.
Shoot with matching in mind: set both cameras to the same framerate, similar shutter (180° rule on both), and the same white balance in the field. Five minutes of discipline on set saves an hour of fighting in post.
On location.
If a ground operator and a drone shoot the same scene, agree on flight paths and 'cut' signals so the drone isn't overhead of the ground crew. Never fly directly over people unless authorized and safe.
▸Hands-On

Cut a matched 20-30s aerial+ground sequence.

  1. Pick one aerial clip and one ground clip of the same subject/location.
  2. Neutralize both with conversion LUTs, then color-match the aerial to the ground using the parade scope.
  3. Intercut them on a single-framerate timeline; cut on motion/beat so pacing flows.
  4. Add one creative look at the timeline level, then export a 20-30 second edit. Note your match steps.
